title: Gum Arabic vs Arabic Gum: Same Thing?
h1: Gum Arabic vs Arabic Gum: Same Thing, Different Name?
description: Gum arabic vs Arabic gum: one ingredient, two word orders. Which name lands on which label, what E414 means, and how to check two packs match.
ogTitle: Gum Arabic vs Arabic Gum: Same Thing, Different Name?
ogDescription: Gum arabic, Arabic gum, acacia gum, acacia fiber, E414, gam arab: one dried acacia sap under six labels. Here is where each name turns up and what it signals.
twitterDescription: Two labels, two names, one ingredient? Read the ingredient line, not the front of the pack. A label-by-label guide to gum arabic and its other names.
excerpt: Same acacia sap, different word order: which of gum arabic, acacia gum, acacia fiber and E414 you meet on which label.
heroCaption: One powder, several names depending on who printed the label.
lede: Gum arabic vs Arabic gum is a naming difference, not an ingredient difference: both names describe the dried, purified sap of the Acacia tree. The word order changes with the market. Gum arabic is the trade name used across the food industry; Arabic Gum is the phrasing Malaysian shoppers say, and the one on the Sihatree pouch.
bodyHtml:
Does the word order change what is inside the jar?

No. Gum arabic and Arabic gum name one material: sap that seeps from the bark of Acacia senegal or Acacia seyal, hardens, is cleaned and milled into a water-soluble powder. Two packs printed with the two word orders can hold contents identical down to the tree they were tapped from.

What the material is, and how much people use, sits in the full guide to what Arabic Gum is.

Which name appears on which kind of label?

It depends on who wrote the label. Food manufacturers and technical documents use gum arabic. American and European panels often print acacia gum or gum acacia. A short additive list may show only E414. Retail fibre tubs say acacia fiber. Malaysian packs, Sihatree included, say Arabic Gum.

Gum arabic and its other names, label by label

Tip

The front of a pack is marketing; the back is regulated labelling. The ingredient line settles a disagreement.

What does E414 on an ingredient panel tell you?

That this gum is in the product, whatever the front of the pack calls it. E414 is the food-additive number for the material, and a number reads the same in every language, so it matches a Malaysian pouch against a European pack printed in French.

The gum is roughly 85% soluble fibre. It holds GRAS status in the United States, and EFSA and JECFA have assessed it as a food additive: safety assessments, not findings about health outcomes, as what the evidence on acacia gum supports sets out.

Is acacia fiber the same product as gum arabic?

On a shop shelf, usually yes. Acacia fiber is a retail name for the milled gum sold as a dietary fibre, and the ingredient behind that label is the same acacia sap. Read the ingredient line, not the product name: it should say gum arabic, acacia gum or E414.

The ingredient line

The regulated name is on the back.

The code E414

One number, every language.

The tree named

Acacia senegal or Acacia seyal, the species.

The form word

Powder or hard pieces describe shape only.

The net weight

The Sihatree pouch holds 150 g.

Not chewing gum

Gum here means dried tree sap.

Why does the Malaysian pack say Arabic Gum instead of gum arabic?

Because that is the word order shoppers here use. The Malay name is gam arab, and Arabic Gum is its closest English reading, so Sihatree Arabic Gum Powder carries it on a 150 g pouch in five flavours. Inside is what a European panel would list as gum arabic or E414.

It is a food, a fibre powder rather than a medicine, sold through Berkat Madinah Store: see the retail and wholesale page.

How do you check two packs hold the same ingredient?

Compare ingredient lines, not front-of-pack names. If both read gum arabic, acacia gum, acacia fiber or E414, you hold one material under two naming conventions. If one lists guar gum, xanthan gum or psyllium husk instead, that is a different plant and a different fibre.

Stop treating two word orders as two products. Check the ingredient line, then compare on form and fibre: start with acacia gum against guar gum.

faqs.q: Why do two sellers spell the same ingredient differently?
faqs.a: Because no rule forces one word order. Gum arabic came into English through the trade route, acacia gum names the tree, and Malaysian listings read Arabic Gum because that is what buyers type. Each seller picks the wording its own market knows.

faqs.q: Is gum acacia just a typo for acacia gum?
faqs.a: No, both orders are in genuine use. Panels in the United States and Europe print gum acacia and acacia gum interchangeably, the way gum arabic and Arabic gum swap places elsewhere. Read all four as one label entry, and confirm with E414 if the panel has it.

faqs.q: What is gum arabic called in Malay?
faqs.a: Gam arab. Malaysian shelf labels, recipes and conversation use that form, and the Sihatree pack reads Serbuk Gam Arab in Malay and Arabic Gum Powder in English. Ask for gam arab at a counter here and you will be understood faster than with gum arabic.

faqs.q: A recipe calls for gum arabic. Can I use a pack labelled acacia gum powder?
faqs.a: The names point at one material, so the question is form rather than identity. Powder is milled and dissolves into liquid; raw gum arrives as hard pieces that must be broken down first. Match the form the recipe asks for, and read the ingredient line before swapping.

faqs.q: Does the name on the pack tell me anything about grade?
faqs.a: Very little. Which name a producer prints reflects the market it sells into, not what is inside. The useful detail sits elsewhere: the ingredient line, the net weight, whether Acacia senegal or Acacia seyal is named, and whether anything besides the gum is listed.

faqs.q: Why does the rest of this site write Arabic Gum rather than gum arabic?
faqs.a: Because the site is written for Malaysia, where Arabic Gum is the phrasing on packs and in conversation, mirroring the Malay gam arab. This page carries the gum arabic word order for readers who search that way, then meet a label using the other.
